# Book I, Proposition 1

*An equilateral triangle on a given line*

> On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/01-idea.svg" alt="Each side of the triangle is a radius of a circle, and the base is a radius of both, so all three sides are equal." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Each side of the triangle is a radius of a circle, and the base is a radius of both, so all three sides are equal.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/01.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.1, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let AB be the given finite straight line.

Thus it is required to construct an equilateral triangle on the straight line AB.

With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; [Post. 3]

again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; [Post. 3]

and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the straight lines CA, CB be joined. [Post. 1]

Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB,

AC is equal to AB. [Def. 15]

Again, since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE,

BC is equal to BA. [Def. 15]

But CA was also proved equal to AB;

therefore each of the straight lines CA, CB is equal to AB.

And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]

therefore CA is also equal to CB.

Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, BC are equal to one another.

Therefore the triangle ABC is equilateral; and it has been constructed on the given finite straight line AB.

(Being) what it was required to do.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop01.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop01.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- What Euclid sees in the figure but never says: the point `C`, being as far
from `A` and from `B` as they are from each other, is not on the straight line
`AB`. So `ABC` really is a triangle. -/
theorem Prop1.figure {A B C : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖A B‖)
    (hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖A B‖) : Triangle A B C := by
  rintro ⟨L, hA, hB, hC⟩
  have hne : ‖A B‖ ≠ 0 := len_ne_zero hAB
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm A C).trans hCA
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm B C).trans hCB
  have hCA' : C ≠ A := fun h => hne (by rw [← hCA, h, len_self])
  have hCB' : C ≠ B := fun h => hne (by rw [← hCB, h, len_self])
  /- On one straight line, one of the three points would lie between the other two,
     and then a length would equal itself taken twice. -/
  rcases between_cases hAB hCB'.symm hCA'.symm hA hB hC with h | h | h
  · have := len_add_of_between h
    rw [hBC, hAC] at this
    exact Magnitude.add_self_ne hne this
  · have := len_add_of_between h
    rw [len_symm B A, hAC, hBC] at this
    exact Magnitude.add_self_ne hne this
  · have := len_add_of_between h
    rw [hAC, hCB] at this
    exact Magnitude.add_self_ne hne this

/-- On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle. -/
theorem Prop1 (A B : Point) (hAB : A ≠ B) :
    ∃ C : Point, Equilateral A B C := by
  -- Let AB be the given finite straight line.
  -- Thus it is required to construct an equilateral triangle on the straight line AB.
  -- With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨BCD, hA_BCD, hB_BCD⟩ := Postulate3 A B hAB
  -- again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨ACE, hB_ACE, hA_ACE⟩ := Postulate3 B A hAB.symm
  -- and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the
  -- straight lines CA, CB be joined. [Post. 1]
  /- Euclid never says why the circles cut one another. Each passes through the
     other's centre, and a centre lies inside its circle, so they must cross
     (System E, Intersection rule 5). Lean needs only the point C; the straight
     lines CA, CB are drawn for the eye. -/
  obtain ⟨C, -, -, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, -⟩ :=
    circles_meet hB_BCD (centre_inside hA_BCD) (centre_inside hB_ACE) hA_ACE
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB,
  -- AC is equal to AB. [Def. 15]
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := Definition15 hA_BCD hC_BCD hB_BCD
  -- Again, since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE,
  -- BC is equal to BA. [Def. 15]
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖B A‖ := Definition15 hB_ACE hC_ACE hA_ACE
  -- But CA was also proved equal to AB;
  have hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C A).trans hAC
  -- therefore each of the straight lines CA, CB is equal to AB.
  have hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C B).trans (hBC.trans (len_symm B A))
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore CA is also equal to CB.
  have hCA_CB : ‖C A‖ = ‖C B‖ := CommonNotion1 hCA hCB
  -- Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, BC are equal to one another.
  have hAB_BC : ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ := (hBC.trans (len_symm B A)).symm
  have hBC_CA : ‖B C‖ = ‖C A‖ := (len_symm B C).trans (hCA_CB.symm)
  -- Therefore the triangle ABC is equilateral; and it has been constructed on the given finite
  -- straight line AB.
  exact ⟨C, Prop1.figure hAB hCA hCB, hAB_BC, hBC_CA⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.
```

<details><summary>The 13 things Euclid takes for granted here</summary>

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L33): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L178): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, then `AB` and `BC` together make up `AC`. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The line `AB` is the line `BA`. (Metric 3)

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L25): Adding is commutative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L44): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L28): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L31): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L38): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L41): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

**The circles that must meet.** Euclid's very first step uses something none of his postulates says: that the two circles cut one another. Heath puts it plainly: "It is a commonplace that Euclid has no right to assume, without premising some postulate, that the two circles will meet in a point C" (vol. 1, p. 242). Here the missing postulate is a named rule, [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean), Intersection rule 5 of the System E of Avigad, Dean and Mumma: if each circle passes through a point inside the other, they cross. It is on the list of things I.1 rests on.

**What the picture shows.** Euclid also never says that C is off the straight line AB, which is what makes ABC a triangle at all. Lean needs it, so `Prop1.figure` proves it: if C were on AB, one of the three points would lie between the other two, and some length would equal itself taken twice.

**The lines CA and CB.** Euclid joins them, citing Postulate 1. Lean needs only the point C, so Postulate 1 is not among the things the Lean proof rests on.

**The modern way.** Put A at 0 and B at 1 in the complex plane. Then C is 1/2 + (√3/2)i, the point you reach by turning AB through 60°. That √3 tells the whole story. In the plane of points with rational coordinates, all five of Euclid's postulates hold, yet the two circles of I.1 slip past each other without meeting, because √3 is not rational. (Robin Hartshorne's *Geometry: Euclid and Beyond* tells this story beautifully.) So the tacit rule is doing real work: it says the plane has the square roots that ruler and compass need.
